name: Bianca Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Bianca. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a small metal fabrication shop, about thirty of us, in an old railway shed on Foundry Row. We make steel frames for café tables and chairs. I run the fibre laser cutter, which cuts shapes out of steel sheet with a beam of light, and the press brake, which folds them. I like the precision, the little click when a fold comes out exactly at ninety degrees. What wears me out is the boss changing orders at four in the afternoon.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you fit AI into that, if at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, honestly. I use an assistant to help me plan how the parts fit on a sheet so we waste less steel, and to translate bits of the laser manual, which is in German. On the side I make custom steel planters and sell them online, and I write all the listings and answer customers with AI help. My partner Jonah is a graphic designer, so we joke that I use the robots and he's scared of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool, nothing magic, and I'd keep using it. I'd probably post something like, see, it's just a better calculator, use it and stop worrying. People at the shop already think I'm a bit obsessed with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be fine with that. My job stays, my planter business keeps growing a bit, Jonah's job stays. If AI stays a clever calculator, I'm the only one at the shop who bothered to learn the buttons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. Keep about ten months saved, put a bit more into the planter business, maybe buy a small second-hand laser for home in a year or so. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved for Jonah, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How big is the planter business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small. Maybe fifteen orders a month, enough to pay for our holidays. I weld them in a rented garage two streets away on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're relieved for Jonah. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because his work is the kind AI is already good at, drawings and layouts. He's had two clients ask for 'something AI-ish' cheaper. If it stalls, he gets to breathe.

S0.say: I'd say AI is a decent tool, nothing magic, and I'd keep using it. I'd tell people it's a better calculator, so use it and stop worrying.
S0.think: Honestly, I'd be fine, because my job, my planter business and Jonah's work would all stay. I'd just be the only one at the shop who bothered to learn the tools.
S0.do: Keeps working, keeps about ten months saved and puts more into her planter business. Might buy a small second-hand laser for home within a year.
S0.feel: Calm, mostly relieved for her partner.
S0.quote: If AI stays a clever calculator, I'm the only one at the shop who bothered to learn the buttons.
S0.fieldNote: Bianca is a daily AI user with a small side business, and her first worry is her partner's design work, not her own job. She's practical and unfussy about the technology. The plateau suits her fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good time to be someone who likes learning. I'd tell my boss we should look at a cobot, a robot arm that works safely beside people, for the press brake. And I'd say people should learn the tools now rather than wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this works out well for me. Small shops like ours will need someone who knows the machines and the software, and that's me. The press brake is the dullest part of my day, and I'd happily hand it to a robot and do the programming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push my boss to try a cobot in the first year and offer to set it up. I'd do a short online course in robot programming. And I'd grow the planter business, maybe double the orders, because I could make them faster with some automation at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even excited. Steady change suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't your boss see the cobot as a reason to need fewer people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but he's always short-staffed. And if I'm the one who runs it, I'm safer than anyone. I'd rather be the person holding the remote.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the shop might struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Petra, who does the welding. She's brilliant but she hates screens. I'd try to get her involved early so she doesn't feel pushed aside.

S1.say: I'd say it's a good time to be someone who likes learning, and I'd suggest my boss gets a cobot for the press brake. People should learn the tools now.
S1.think: I think steady change works out well for me, because small shops will need someone who knows both the machines and the software. That's me.
S1.do: Pushes her boss to try a cobot in the first year and offers to set it up. Takes an online robot programming course and grows the planter business with some home automation.
S1.feel: Calm and excited, since steady change suits her.
S1.quote: The press brake is the dullest part of my day, and I'd happily hand it to a robot and do the programming.
S1.fieldNote: Bianca would happily hand her dullest task to a robot and take over its programming. She frames being the operator of the new kit as her job security. She thinks about a colleague who avoids screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and nobody's ready, and that we need some kind of plan for people whose jobs go overnight. I'd still say I'm not against the technology. I'd just say this speed isn't fair on people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it hits both of us at once. My shop job goes, Jonah's design work goes, and even my planters, well, a robot could make and sell them cheaper. That's the one I hadn't thought about until now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder straight away and go all in on the planter business while I still could, maybe get it to sixty orders a month. I'd put some money into a small laser and robot welder for it, so at least I'd own the machines. And I'd look at jobs where people still want a person, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. For the first time I'd feel like being good with AI doesn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy machines for the planters. Isn't that risky if AI can make them cheaper anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. But if the robots are going to win, I'd rather own two of them than be replaced by somebody else's. It's a bet, and I'd keep it small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years' notice, what would you say to Jonah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we need to stop pretending it'll pass. We'd sit down at the kitchen table and go through our money, and plan what we'd live on if both of us stopped earning. We're lucky, we've got savings, but two years isn't long.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast and nobody's ready, and people whose jobs vanish overnight need a plan. I'm not against the technology, but this speed isn't fair.
S2.think: It hits both of us at once: my shop job goes and Jonah's design work goes. Even my planters could be made and sold cheaper by a robot, which I hadn't thought about until now.
S2.do: Saves harder and grows the planter business fast, investing in a small laser and robot welder so she owns the machines. Also looks at jobs where people still want a person.
S2.feel: Anxious, feeling for the first time that being good with AI doesn't help.
S2.quote: if the robots are going to win, I'd rather own two of them than be replaced by somebody else's.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI is the first picture where Bianca's AI skills stop protecting her, and she says so. She responds by buying machines rather than fearing them. Her worry is shared with her partner, whose job would go too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years, so let's use them well. The government should be planning now, and businesses should be honest about what's coming. I'd say people like me should get ready to run our own small shops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough to build something of my own. I'd be thirty-two. If I get the planter business big enough, with its own machines, I'd at least own something when the jobs go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the shop job for the steady money and build the planter business on the side. In the first year I'd buy a second-hand laser and learn some design, maybe with Jonah's help. By year three I'd want it bringing in as much as my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but busy. Too busy to really worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the difference between grabbing and building. With two years I'd be throwing money at machines in a panic. With five, I'd have time to find out what customers actually want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you bring Jonah into the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. He could design the planters, I'd make them. It'd be a way to keep both our skills useful for a bit longer, even if AI does designs too.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years, so let's use them well: governments should plan now and businesses should be honest. People like me should get ready to run our own small shops.
S3.think: Five years is enough for me to build a business of my own, with its own machines. That way I'd at least own something when the jobs go.
S3.do: Keeps the shop job for steady pay while building the planter business. Buys a second-hand laser in the first year, learns design and aims for the business to match her wage by year three.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but too busy to really worry.
S3.quote: With two years I'd be throwing money at machines in a panic. With five, I'd have time to find out what customers actually want.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Bianca shifts from grabbing to building, a phrase she uses herself. She sees bringing her partner into the business as a way to keep both of them useful. Ownership is her main answer to the threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance, and people should use it to learn and to build. I'd say the government should help people start small businesses, not just hand out training vouchers. Same message, more time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years makes me feel okay. I'd have time to grow the planters into a proper little business, automate it myself, and maybe leave the shop. It might all get undercut in the end, but I'd have ten good years first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the business steadily, buy machines in years one to three, and leave the shop around year four or five. I'd keep investing in the business and keep savings for at least a year. And I'd keep using AI for everything, because the better I get, the cheaper I can run things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd feel ready, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd leave a steady job for a planter business. Isn't that a big risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, but by year four I'd know if it worked. If it didn't, there'd still be shops needing laser operators for a few more years. I'd only jump once the numbers said yes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would stop you feeling calm in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Jonah ended up struggling and I couldn't help. My plan works for me, but I don't want to be the one doing fine while the person I love is lost.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a real chance to learn and build, and governments should help people start small businesses, not just hand out training vouchers.
S4.think: Ten years makes me feel okay, because I'd have time to grow and automate my own business and maybe leave the shop. It might get undercut in the end, but I'd have ten good years first.
S4.do: Grows the planter business, buys machines in years one to three and leaves the shop around year four or five once the numbers work. Keeps a year of savings and uses AI daily to run things cheaply.
S4.quote: My plan works for me, but I don't want to be the one doing fine while the person I love is lost.
S4.fieldNote: Bianca feels ready for the ten-year picture, with a clear plan to own and automate her own business. Her one real worry is her partner, not herself. She'll only jump once the numbers say yes, which is careful for someone who likes risk.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because both me and Jonah would be hit at the same time, and there'd be no time to build anything. Being good with the tools only helps if there's time to use them. What would help is support for people starting small businesses, cheap loans for machines, and help for creative people like Jonah to find new work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how couples deal with it. Everyone thinks about one job at a time, but it's households. If both people are hit at once, that's a different story.

headlineQuote: Being good with the tools only helps if there's time to use them.
portrait: Bianca is a 27-year-old laser and press brake operator at a small metal fabrication shop, using AI daily at work and for her side business selling steel planters online. She lives with her partner Jonah, a graphic designer whose work is more exposed to AI than hers. She stays calm through the plateau and steady disruption, even wanting to automate her own dullest task, but fast AGI makes her anxious because her AI skills stop protecting her. With more time her answer is ownership: build and automate her own business, while worrying mostly about Jonah.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most because she and Jonah would be hit at the same time, with no time to build anything.
whatWouldHelp: Support for people starting small businesses, cheap loans for machines, and help for creative workers like Jonah to find new work.
